scenes.animation: A futuristic bedroom with a glowing screen. An eleven-year-old girl, Margie, scribbles in her diary: 'May 17, 2157. Today Tommy found a real book!' Zippy gasps as an ancient, yellowed paper book floats into view like a museum treasure.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Finding a real book is big news? What kind of world is this?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The year 2157, in Isaac Asimov's story The Fun They Had. Books are on screens, and even teachers are machines.

scenes.animation: Tommy, thirteen, flips the crinkly pages; the words stand still on the page. Margie compares it with her telescreen where words move. Tommy grins: 'Centuries ago'. A caption: 'The book is about school'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Margie is eleven and her friend Tommy is thirteen. The old book is about school, the way it was centuries ago.

lines.speaker: TOMMY
lines.text: What a waste. When you're through with the book, you just throw it away.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He means their telescreen holds a million books, and you never throw it away.

scenes.animation: Margie's schoolroom right next to her bedroom: a big black mechanical teacher with a screen and a slot for homework. A red-faced County Inspector opens it with a box of tools and slows the geography sector to an average ten-year level.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Margie hates school. Her mechanical teacher kept giving her geography test after test, and she did worse and worse.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the County Inspector took it apart and slowed the geography sector to an average ten-year level.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A teacher you can repair with a screwdriver. That's both cool and creepy.

scenes.animation: Split screen. Left: Margie alone, inserting homework into a slot in a punch code. Right: a sepia old school with a building, a human teacher and children laughing and shouting in the yard, going home together.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Margie is amazed to read that children once went to a special building, all learning the same things, taught by a man.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: They sat together, laughed and shouted in the schoolyard, and went home together.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: As her machine drones on about fractions, Margie thinks about the fun they had.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Why did Margie hate school? Why did she think the old kind of school was fun?' Answer points build: 'Lonely mechanical teacher', 'No friends in class', 'Shared learning, play, human teacher'. A 'Board Tip' sticker glows.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: why did Margie hate school, and why did she think the old schools were fun?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: she studied alone with a machine that tested her again and again. Old schools had friends, play, and a human teacher.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: connect it to the theme. Technology can teach, but learning is richer when it is shared.

scenes.animation: Recap board with an old book and a glowing screen side by side. Points appear: '1. 2157: Tommy finds a real book about old schools', '2. Margie studies alone with a mechanical teacher', '3. She longs for the fun of learning together'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: in 2157, Tommy finds a real book about old schools.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Margie studies alone with a mechanical teacher, and she hates it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: she longs for the fun of learning with friends.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'm hugging my real classmates tomorrow. Even the noisy ones.

scenes.animation: A concert stage. A barefoot percussionist strikes a marimba; visible vibration waves travel up through the floor into her feet. Zippy covers his ears, then uncovers them in confusion.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is she playing barefoot? Did she forget her shoes?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. She feels the music through her body. Meet Evelyn Glennie, from part one of The Sound of Music.

scenes.animation: A Scottish school. Young Evelyn's report card marks drop; a doctor's chart shows a fading sound-wave: 'severe hearing loss'. Then a percussion teacher, Ron Forbes, tunes two drums to different notes and taps her hand on each.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: By the time Evelyn was eleven, her marks had fallen. Doctors found her hearing was severely damaged, and she was told to get hearing aids and go to a school for the deaf.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Instead, percussionist Ron Forbes noticed her talent. He tuned two drums to different notes and told her to sense them, not listen with her ears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: She learned to feel higher notes in her upper body and lower notes from the waist down. She went on to the Royal Academy of Music in London.

scenes.animation: A royal court with a scowling Emperor Aurangzeb banning the shrill pungi. A barber from a musicians' family redesigns it into a longer pipe with holes; the royal chamber fills with sweet sound. Label: 'shah + nai = shehnai'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Part two is about the shehnai. Emperor Aurangzeb had banned the shrill pungi. A barber improved it, played it in the royal chamber, and it came to be called the shehnai.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Its greatest master was Ustad Bismillah Khan, born in 1916 in Dumraon, Bihar. As a boy he practised for hours in the temples of Benaras and on the banks of the Ganga.

scenes.animation: The Red Fort on 15 August 1947; a shehnai's notes rise over a crowd with tricolours. Then a montage: a film reel, a world map with concert pins, a Bharat Ratna medal. Finally, the Ganga at Benaras glows.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: On 15 August 1947, he played the shehnai at the Red Fort as India became independent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He performed across the world and received the Bharat Ratna, but he refused to leave Benaras and the Ganga.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Two musicians, two very different paths, and both refused to give up.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. How did Evelyn Glennie overcome her disability? What values do both musicians share?' Answer tags attach: 'determination', 'hard work', 'love for music', 'love for roots'. A 'Board Tip' sticker appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: how did Evelyn overcome her hearing loss?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: mention Ron Forbes's help, her learning to sense sound through her body, and her sheer determination.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in a value question, compare both musicians: dedication to their art, and in Bismillah Khan's case, deep love for his roots.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a drum and a shehnai. Points appear: '1. Evelyn Glennie feels music through her body', '2. The shehnai grew from the banned pungi', '3. Bismillah Khan: Red Fort 1947, Bharat Ratna, loyal to Benaras'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Evelyn Glennie overcame deafness by feeling music through her body.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the shehnai grew out of the pungi that Aurangzeb banned.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: Bismillah Khan played at the Red Fort in 1947, won the Bharat Ratna, and stayed loyal to Benaras.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'm taking my shoes off before music class from now on.

scenes.animation: A little girl, Kezia, peeps from behind the stairs as a big shadow of her father fills the hallway. As he leaves in a buggy, she lets out a huge sigh of relief and sags like a deflated balloon.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is she so relieved when her father leaves? Is he a monster?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: To Kezia, he almost is. This is Katherine Mansfield's story, The Little Girl.

scenes.animation: At the dinner table, the father's voice booms; Kezia's speech bubble breaks into stuttering fragments 'I... I...'. A caption: 'Stern father, frightened child'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Kezia is afraid of her father. He is strict and stern, and in front of him she begins to stutter.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Her grandmother, whom she loves, suggests a birthday present for him: a pincushion.

scenes.animation: Kezia happily stuffs a pincushion with torn paper from her mother's room. Later, the father storms in, holding up empty pages: 'my great speech for the Port Authority'. He brings out a ruler; Kezia holds out her hands and cries.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: She stuffs it with papers she finds in her mother's room. But those papers were his great speech for the Port Authority.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He punishes her by hitting her palms with a ruler, to teach her not to touch what does not belong to her.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Ouch. And she was only trying to be nice.

scenes.animation: Over the fence, the Macdonald family plays: the father gives children rides on his shoulders and tickles them till they get hiccups. Kezia watches wide-eyed; the caption reads 'different sorts of fathers'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Next door, Mr. Macdonald plays with his children and makes them laugh. Kezia decides there are different sorts of fathers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then one night, her mother is ill in hospital, and her grandmother has gone with her. Kezia has a nightmare about a butcher with a knife and wakes up screaming.

scenes.animation: Night. The father carries Kezia to his big bed and tucks her in. She rests her head on his chest; a soft heartbeat pulses on screen. He is shown tired and asleep. Her fear melts into a warm glow.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It is her father who comes, picks her up and lets her sleep beside him. She sees how tired he is after working so hard.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Resting her head on his chest, she says: what a big heart you've got, father dear.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. How does Kezia's attitude towards her father change?' Arrows move from 'fear' to 'understanding' to 'love'. Sticker: 'Board Tip: give the turning point'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: how does Kezia's view of her father change, and why?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: from fear to understanding. The turning point is the night he comforts her. Exam tip: mention that parents may be strict yet loving underneath.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a pincushion and a heart. Points appear: '1. Kezia fears her stern father', '2. The pincushion mistake and punishment', '3. After the nightmare, she sees his big heart'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Kezia fears her stern father.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: her pincushion gift destroys his speech, and he punishes her.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: after her nightmare, he comforts her, and she discovers his big heart.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Note to self: check the paper before you stuff a pincushion.

scenes.animation: A playground in 1880s Germany. Children point at a quiet boy building a tall house of cards and giggle 'Brother Boring!'. The boy calmly adds one more card; the tower stands perfectly.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: They call him Brother Boring? He looks like he's thinking about the universe.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He is. That boy is Albert Einstein, and his biography in your book is called A Truly Beautiful Mind.

scenes.animation: A map pins 'Ulm, Germany, 1879'. Then a strict Munich classroom with ticking clocks and marching desks; young Albert frowns. An arrow shows him leaving for Switzerland; a sign reads 'Zurich'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Einstein was born in Ulm, Germany, in 1879. He started speaking late, and his playmates called him Brother Boring.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He disliked the strict, regimented school in Munich, and later went to Switzerland, where he studied in Zurich.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: There he met Mileva Maric, a fellow student, whom he later married.

scenes.animation: A patent office desk piled with files. Einstein secretly scribbles equations; the glowing formula 'E = mc²' floats up from the page. A calendar flips to 1905.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Unable to get a university job, he worked as a technical expert in the patent office in Bern.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In his spare time he worked on physics. In 1905 he published his special theory of relativity, which led to the famous formula E equals m c squared.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: He changed science from a patent office desk? That's my kind of multitasking.

scenes.animation: A newspaper headline about the general theory proved by a solar eclipse. Then a darker scene: a 1939 letter addressed to President Roosevelt; a mushroom cloud over Hiroshima; Einstein's sad face; a dove flying towards the United Nations building.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: His general theory of relativity made him world-famous. But when Hitler came to power, Einstein, who was Jewish, left Germany for America.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1939 he wrote to President Roosevelt, warning that Germany might build an atom bomb. After the bombing of Hiroshima, he was deeply shocked and worked for world peace until he died in 1955.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Why is Einstein called a "truly beautiful mind"?' Answer points build: 'brilliant scientist', 'independent thinker', 'worked for peace'. Sticker: 'Board Tip: link genius with humanity'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: why is Einstein called a truly beautiful mind?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: mention his genius in science, his independent thinking, and his campaign for peace after the bomb.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: remember that his letter to Roosevelt was a warning, not a wish to see the bomb used.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the house of cards and E = mc². Points appear: '1. Born in Ulm, 1879; called Brother Boring', '2. Patent office, 1905: special relativity', '3. Warned Roosevelt; worked for peace; died 1955'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Einstein was born in Ulm in 1879 and was called Brother Boring.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: while at the patent office, he published the special theory of relativity in 1905.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: he warned Roosevelt about the bomb and later worked for peace.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Brother Boring, huh? Best comeback ever: change physics.

scenes.animation: A tiny rented room with a tiled roof and rafters. A young doctor admires himself in a mirror, twirling an imaginary moustache. Above him, a cobra peers down from the rafters. Zippy clamps his hands over his mouth.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Someone tell him to look up! Look up!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He's too busy admiring himself. This is Vaikom Muhammad Basheer's funny and scary story, The Snake and the Mirror.

scenes.animation: The doctor, a poor homeopath, counts a few coins by lamplight. He grins at the mirror; thought-bubbles show a handsome moustache, a daily shave, and a smiling fat lady doctor with bags of money.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The narrator is a young homeopath who earns very little and lives in a rented room.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One hot night, looking in the mirror, he decides to shave every day, grow a thin moustache, and always smile to look handsome.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He even dreams of marrying a fat lady doctor with plenty of money.

scenes.animation: Thud! The snake drops onto his shoulder and coils around his left arm, its hood close to his face. The doctor freezes like a stone statue; a heartbeat thumps loudly; sweat drops fall in slow motion.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Suddenly, a snake falls from the rafters onto his shoulder and coils around his left arm.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He sits absolutely still, like a stone image, hardly breathing, and prays to God.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: No more moustache plans now, I bet.

scenes.animation: The snake slowly uncoils, slides to the table and gazes at its own reflection in the mirror. The doctor tiptoes out and runs into the night. The next morning, he finds the room emptied by a thief, except for a dirty vest.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then the snake turns its head, sees itself in the mirror, and moves towards it, as if admiring its own looks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The doctor slips out and runs. The next morning, a thief has taken almost everything from his room, except his dirty vest.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. What is the source of humour in the story?' Answer tags appear: 'vanity of the doctor', 'snake also admires itself', 'thief leaves the dirty vest'. Sticker: 'Board Tip: humour + fear'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: how does the writer mix humour with fear?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: the doctor's vanity at the mirror, the snake seeming to admire itself just as he did, and the funny twist with the vest.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: mention the theme too. Vanity looks silly when life is in danger.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a small mirror and a coiled snake. Points appear: '1. A poor, vain young doctor', '2. A snake coils around his arm; he freezes', '3. The snake turns to the mirror; he escapes'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a poor young homeopath admires himself in the mirror.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: a snake falls on him and coils around his arm, and he freezes in terror.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the snake turns to the mirror, and the doctor escapes.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Moral of the story: check the ceiling before checking your face.

scenes.animation: A railway platform in Rameswaram in the 1940s. A train rushes past without stopping; a bundle of newspapers is flung out. A thin boy with bright eyes sprints to catch it and grins.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is that boy chasing newspapers thrown from a train?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's how he earned his first wages. The boy is A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, and this is My Childhood.

scenes.animation: A sturdy house on Mosque Street, Rameswaram. Kalam's father sits calmly; his mother serves food to many guests. Labels: 'Father: Jainulabdeen, honest, self-disciplined', 'Mother: Ashiamma, kind'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Kalam was born in Rameswaram, in a middle-class Tamil family. His father, Jainulabdeen, was honest and self-disciplined; his mother was generous and kind.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: During the Second World War, he earned money helping his cousin Samsuddin distribute newspapers.

scenes.animation: A classroom. A new teacher glares at a Muslim cap and a sacred thread side by side on the front bench, and sends Kalam to the back. Ramanadha Sastry sits in tears. Later, his father, the temple priest, confronts the teacher.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: His close friend Ramanadha Sastry was the son of the high priest of the Rameswaram temple.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A new teacher could not bear a Hindu priest's son sitting with a Muslim boy, and moved Kalam to the back bench.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ramanadha's father, Lakshmana Sastry, told the teacher to apologise or leave. The teacher changed his ways.

scenes.animation: Science teacher Sivasubramania Iyer's kitchen. His wife refuses to serve a Muslim boy; Iyer serves Kalam himself and eats beside him. Next week, his wife serves Kalam with her own hands.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: His science teacher, Sivasubramania Iyer, invited him home for a meal. His wife refused to serve a Muslim boy in her kitchen, so Iyer served him himself.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The next week, she served him inside her kitchen. Change had begun.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: One brave teacher changed a whole kitchen's rules!

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. How did Kalam's teachers and elders fight social barriers?' Answer points: 'Lakshmana Sastry corrects the teacher', 'Iyer serves Kalam', 'Father lets him leave to study'. Sticker: 'Board Tip: quote examples'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: When Kalam wished to study at Ramanathapuram, his parents let him go, though it was hard for them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: how were social barriers broken in young Kalam's world? Answer approach: give both examples, the priest and the science teacher.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: link them to the theme of religious harmony and good values at home.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a newspaper bundle and a temple and mosque side by side. Points appear: '1. Rameswaram childhood; honest, loving parents', '2. First wages from newspapers', '3. Elders and teachers broke barriers of caste and religion'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Kalam grew up in Rameswaram with honest, loving parents.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: he earned his first wages distributing newspapers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: his elders and teachers broke barriers of religion and taught him harmony.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: From catching newspapers to making headlines. Now that's a story.

scenes.animation: Snowy summit of Mount Everest. A woman plants the Indian tricolour, then the scene rewinds a year and shows her doing it again. A counter clicks '1... 2!'. Zippy's jaw drops.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: She climbed Everest twice? I get tired climbing to the fourth floor!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's Santosh Yadav, from part one of Reach for the Top. Part two is about tennis star Maria Sharapova.

scenes.animation: A village in Haryana. Little Santosh in shorts refuses to wear a traditional dress. Later, she sits at a school desk in Delhi, then a college hostel in Jaipur, watching climbers disappear up the hills.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Santosh was born in Joniyawas, a village in Haryana, the only girl among five brothers. She refused to follow the tradition of early marriage.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: She insisted on studying, went to school in Delhi, and later to Maharani College in Jaipur, where she watched climbers on the Aravalli hills.

scenes.animation: A mountaineering institute sign in Uttarkashi. Santosh trains, then on Everest she shares her oxygen with a struggling climber. Pins appear: '1992' and '1993'. Then she carries sacks of garbage down the slopes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: She joined a mountaineering course at Uttarkashi. In 1992 she climbed Everest, and within a year, she did it again, becoming the only woman to scale it twice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: On the mountain she shared her oxygen to help a fellow climber, and she brought down five hundred kilograms of garbage from the Himalayas.

scenes.animation: A Russian girl of nine says goodbye to her mother at an airport and flies with her father to America. She trains on sunlit courts, lonely at night. Later, a scoreboard shows 'World Number One'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Maria Sharapova was sent from Russia to America at just nine years old to train in tennis. Her mother could not come, and they were apart for two years.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: She faced loneliness and hard training, and became the world's number one tennis player while still a teenager.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Two continents, one message: sacrifice now, summit later.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. What qualities do Santosh Yadav and Maria Sharapova share?' Tags attach: 'determination', 'hard work', 'sacrifice', 'confidence'. Sticker: 'Board Tip: one example for each quality'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: what qualities do the two women share?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: name qualities like determination, hard work and sacrifice, and support each with an example from their lives.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: don't mix up the details. Everest twice is Santosh; leaving home at nine is Maria.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a mountain flag and a tennis racquet. Points appear: '1. Santosh Yadav: Everest twice, 1992 and 1993', '2. Helped a climber, cleaned the Himalayas', '3. Maria Sharapova: training from age nine to world number one'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Santosh Yadav climbed Everest twice, in 1992 and 1993.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: she helped a fellow climber and cleared Himalayan garbage.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: Maria Sharapova left home at nine and rose to world number one.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Right. Starting today, I'm reaching for the top shelf. Of the snack cupboard.

scenes.animation: A crowded temple courtyard in Nepal: priests, hawkers, tourists, cows, monkeys and pigeons all at once. Two monkeys chase each other across the scene. Zippy dodges a monkey and lands in a flower basket.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Priests, cows, monkeys, tourists, all in one place? Where are we?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Kathmandu, with the travel writer Vikram Seth. This chapter comes from his book Heaven Lake.

scenes.animation: Pashupatinath temple with a sign 'Entrance for the Hindus only'. The Bagmati river flows by; washerwomen work, a body burns on the bank, a basket of flowers floats past. A small shrine half sticks out of a stone platform.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: First he visits Pashupatinath, a Hindu temple. There is an atmosphere of feverish confusion: priests, hawkers, devotees, tourists and animals.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: By the holy Bagmati river, a body is being burnt while washerwomen work nearby.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A small shrine sticks halfway out of a stone platform. People believe that when it fully emerges, the evil age of Kali Yuga will end.

scenes.animation: A calm white dome of the Baudhnath stupa under a blue sky, prayer flags fluttering. Around it, small Tibetan shops sell felt bags, prints and silver jewellery. The noisy soundtrack fades into stillness.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Next, the Baudhnath stupa, a Buddhist shrine. In contrast, it has a sense of stillness.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Its huge white dome is ringed by a road with small shops, many run by Tibetan immigrants.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So one place is a festival, and the other is a deep breath.

scenes.animation: A busy Kathmandu street with cheap goods and music. The author munches roasted corn and marzipan. A flute seller stands with a pole of flutes sticking out like a porcupine's quills and plays a slow tune; the street seems to pause.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The city's streets are noisy and busy. After buying snacks and comics, the author decides to return to Delhi by bus and train.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then he notices a flute seller with a pole of flutes like a porcupine. He plays slowly and calmly, and the author reflects that the flute is found in almost every culture.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Compare the atmosphere at Pashupatinath and Baudhnath.' A two-column table fills: 'Pashupatinath: noisy, crowded, confused' vs 'Baudhnath: quiet, peaceful, still'. Sticker: 'Board Tip: use contrast words'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: compare the atmosphere at Pashupatinath and Baudhnath.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: Pashupatinath is crowded and chaotic; Baudhnath is quiet and still. Use words like whereas and in contrast.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: remember which shrine is Hindu and which is Buddhist. Students often swap them.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a temple and a stupa side by side, and a flute on top. Points appear: '1. Pashupatinath: Hindu, crowded, feverish', '2. Baudhnath: Buddhist, calm, still', '3. The flute: a universal music'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: Pashupatinath is a crowded Hindu temple by the Bagmati.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the Baudhnath stupa is a calm Buddhist shrine.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the flute seller's music reminds the author that music unites all cultures.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And I'm keeping away from those monkeys.

scenes.animation: A lonely cottage at night. Gerrard, a well-dressed man, is on the phone. Behind him, a door creaks and a masked Intruder steps in holding a revolver. Theatre curtains frame the scene: 'A play by Douglas James'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A stranger with a gun, and that man is still so calm?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's Gerrard, and his calm is his weapon. This is the play If I Were You.

scenes.animation: The Intruder circles Gerrard, comparing their faces in a mirror. Thought-bubble: the Intruder wearing Gerrard's clothes, driving his car. A caption: 'The plan: kill Gerrard, become Gerrard'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Intruder is a criminal on the run from the police for murder. He looks rather like Gerrard.

lines.speaker: INTRUDER
lines.text: I'm going to kill you and take your identity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He plans to shoot Gerrard and live as him, since Gerrard lives alone and few people know him.

scenes.animation: Gerrard leans back, smirking, and spins a story. Around him appear fake 'wanted' posters with his own face and a police car's flashing light outside the window. The Intruder's confidence cracks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Gerrard stays cool and uses his wits. He claims that he himself is a crook, wanted by the police.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So if the Intruder becomes Gerrard, he will be caught for Gerrard's crimes. The police, he says, may already be on the way.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Ha! Stealing his identity just became a terrible idea.

scenes.animation: Gerrard points to a door, saying it leads out. The Intruder rushes through it; it's a cupboard. Gerrard slams it shut and locks it. Muffled shouts. Gerrard picks up the phone, smiling.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The panicking Intruder wants to escape. Gerrard shows him a door as a way out, but it is really a cupboard, and Gerrard locks him in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then he calmly calls the police, and jokes on the phone that he might use this in his next play.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. How does Gerrard outwit the Intruder?' Answer points: 'stays calm', 'invents a false criminal past', 'traps him in the cupboard'. Sticker: 'Board Tip: character sketch with evidence'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: how does Gerrard outwit the Intruder?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: he stays calm, invents a false story that makes the plan dangerous, and traps the Intruder in a cupboard.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in a character sketch, call Gerrard witty, calm and quick-thinking, and back each quality with an event.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a locked cupboard door and a telephone. Points appear: '1. Intruder plans to kill Gerrard and take his identity', '2. Gerrard claims he is wanted by the police', '3. Gerrard traps the Intruder in a cupboard'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the Intruder plans to kill Gerrard and become him.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Gerrard invents a criminal past to make the plan dangerous.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: he tricks the Intruder into a cupboard and calls the police.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Brains beat bullets. If I were the Intruder, I'd have stayed home.
